title: Acts of the Apostles
summary: The fifth book of the New Testament and the second volume of Luke's two-part work: the story of how the risen Jesus' witnesses, empowered by the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, carried the message about him from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the Gentiles and finally to Rome, centred first on Peter and then on Paul.
studyQuestions: Compare Luke 1:1-4 with Acts 1:1-3. Who is addressed in both, and what does Acts say the "former treatise" was about?
Acts 1:8 names Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and "the uttermost part of the earth." Trace where the story is in chapters 2, 8, 10 and 28. How does the book follow that map?
What question brought the apostles and elders together in Acts 15:1-6, and how does the phrase "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us" (15:28) describe the way they reached a decision?

Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome yet preaching "with all boldness, none forbidding him" (28:31). Why might Luke end there rather than with Paul's trial, and what does that say about the ongoing story the church still lives in?

title: Babylonian Exile
summary: The deportation of the people of Judah to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar II in the early sixth century BC — in waves around 597 and 587/586 BC, with the burning of Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple — until Cyrus of Persia allowed exiles to return in 538 BC; the crisis that reshaped Israel's faith and much of the Old Testament.
studyQuestions: According to 2 Kings 24:10-16 and 25:8-12, who was taken to Babylon in each deportation, and who was left behind in the land?
What does Jeremiah tell the exiles to do in Jeremiah 29:4-7, and why might that have surprised people who expected to go home soon?
Psalm 137 asks how anyone can sing the Lord's song in a foreign land. How do Ezekiel 1:1-3 and Isaiah 40:1-2 answer that question in different ways?
Matthew 1:17 divides Jesus's family tree at the exile. What does that tell you about how the first Christians understood where Jesus fits in Israel's story?

1 Peter 1:1 and 1:17 call Christians foreigners and exiles. Where do you feel "away from home" in your own life or church, and what would it look like to seek the peace of the place where God has put you?

title: Barnabas
summary: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, "Son of Encouragement"; a generous early member of the Jerusalem church who vouched for the newly converted Saul, led the young church at Antioch and was sent out with Paul on the first missionary journey.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 4:36-37, what was Barnabas's real name, where was he from, and what did he do with his field?
In Acts 9:26-27, why were the disciples in Jerusalem afraid of Saul, and what did Barnabas tell the apostles about him?
What did Barnabas see when he arrived in Antioch (Acts 11:22-24), and how did he respond?
Compare the order of the names in Acts 13:2 and 13:7 with Acts 13:46. What change in the mission does it hint at?
Barnabas gave Mark a second chance after Mark had left the work (Acts 15:36-39). Who in your church or life might need someone to vouch for them, and what would it cost you to do it?

title: Biblical Canon
summary: The list of books a church receives as Holy Scripture: the "measuring rod" collection that makes up the Old and New Testaments, recognised gradually over centuries and still slightly different in size among Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians.
studyQuestions: In Luke 24:44, which three groups of writings does the risen Jesus say speak about him?
How does 2 Peter 3:15-16 describe Paul's letters, and what does that suggest about how early Christians regarded them?
Why might it matter that the canon was recognised gradually by the whole church, rather than chosen in a single meeting?
If your Bible has fewer or more Old Testament books than a friend's from another tradition, how could you talk about the difference with charity and accuracy?

title: Book of Ezra
summary: The Old Testament book that tells how Jewish exiles returned from Babylon under the Persian king Cyrus, rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, and were later led by Ezra, a priest and scribe, to reorder their life around the Law of Moses; in the Hebrew Bible it forms one book with Nehemiah.
studyQuestions: Compare Ezra 1:1-4 with 2 Chronicles 36:22-23. What do the two passages share, and what does that suggest about how the story of Israel continues after the exile?
In Ezra 3:10-13, why do some people shout for joy while older priests and Levites weep at the laying of the Temple's foundation?
What stopped the rebuilding in Ezra 4:24, and according to Ezra 6:14, through whose prophesying did the elders build and prosper?
Ezra 7:10 says Ezra set his heart to seek the law, to do it and to teach it. Why do you think the order of those three verbs matters for anyone who studies Scripture?
Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 confesses the sins of the whole community, not just his own. What might it look like for a church to pray that way today?

title: Book of Jeremiah
summary: The Old Testament prophetic book that gathers the oracles, prayers and life story of Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth who warned Judah from about 627 BC until after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC, wrote to the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon, and promised a new covenant written on the heart.
studyQuestions: In Jeremiah 1:4-10, what objection does Jeremiah raise to God's call, and what two kinds of work (tearing down and building up) is he given?
According to Jeremiah 7:1-15, why could the Temple not protect the people of Judah, and what did God want from them instead?
What does Jeremiah 29:4-7 tell the exiles to do in Babylon, and how does verse 11 read differently once you know it was written to people facing seventy years away from home?
Read Jeremiah 31:31-34 alongside Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:8-13. What is "new" about the new covenant, and how do the New Testament writers see it fulfilled?
In Jeremiah 20:7-18 the prophet both praises God and curses the day he was born. What does it mean to you that such honest prayers are part of Scripture?
Jeremiah buys a field in a city under siege (Jeremiah 32:6-15). Where might God be asking you or your church to act in hope when circumstances look bleak?

title: Forgiveness in the Bible
summary: What Scripture says to Christians who need to forgive, or to be forgiven: God's forgiveness of sin, freely given and proclaimed from Exodus 34 to the cross, and Jesus's call for his followers to forgive others from the heart as they have been forgiven, without pretending that harm did not happen.
studyQuestions: How does God describe himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6-7, and what does that tell us about where forgiveness begins?
In Matthew 18:21-35, how large is the first servant's debt compared with what his fellow servant owes him, and what point is Jesus making by the contrast?
Luke 17:3-4 speaks of rebuking a brother who sins and forgiving him when he repents. How does that fit with Jesus praying for those crucifying him in Luke 23:34?
What did Joseph's forgiveness of his brothers in Genesis 50:15-21 include, and what did it not pretend?
Is there someone I find hard to forgive? What would it look like to begin by praying for them, even before my feelings change?

title: Gospel of Luke
summary: The third Gospel and the first volume of Luke's two-part work with Acts: an orderly account, written for Theophilus, of Jesus' birth, Spirit-anointed ministry, long journey to Jerusalem, death, resurrection and ascension, presenting him as the Saviour who seeks and saves the lost and brings good news to the poor and to all peoples.
studyQuestions: Read Luke 1:1-4. What does Luke say about how he gathered his material, and why does he say he is writing to Theophilus?
In the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16-21) Jesus reads from Isaiah 61. Who is the good news for, and what does he say has happened "today"?

Luke 15 opens with a complaint that Jesus "receiveth sinners, and eateth with them" (15:2). How do the three stories that follow answer it, and why does the last one end with the elder brother still outside?
In Luke 10:29 the lawyer asks "who is my neighbor?", but in 10:36 Jesus asks which man "proved neighbor". How does that change of question change the way you read the parable?
Luke 24 ends with the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures to his disciples (24:27, 44-45). How might reading the Old Testament "concerning himself" shape the way you read it this week?

title: Gospel of Matthew
summary: The first book of the New Testament: an account of the life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus that presents him as Israel's Messiah, Son of David and Son of God, organised around five great teaching discourses and closing with the commission to make disciples of all nations.
studyQuestions: Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham." Why might Matthew open with those two names in particular?
Find the sentence that closes each of the five teaching blocks (Matthew 7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1). What does each discourse teach disciples about life in the kingdom?
In Matthew 5:17-20, what does Jesus say he came to do with the Law and the Prophets, and what kind of righteousness does he ask of his followers?
The Gospel begins with "God with us" (1:23) and ends with "I am with you always" (28:20). How does that promise frame everything in between, and where do you need to hear it this week?

title: Grace
summary: God's free, undeserved favour and the gift of his saving and transforming life, traced in Scripture from God's favour to Noah and his self-description as "merciful and gracious" in Exodus 34 to the grace that comes through Jesus Christ and saves "through faith"; Christian traditions agree that salvation begins in grace but describe how grace works in different ways.
studyQuestions: Exodus 34:6 is God's own description of himself to Moses. Which words in it describe grace, and why is it striking that this comes right after the golden calf?
According to Ephesians 2:8-10, what saves us, what does not, and what are we then created for?
In Romans 6:1-2, what wrong conclusion does Paul expect someone to draw from "grace abounded", and how does he answer it?
Paul hears "My grace is sufficient for you" in a time of weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Where in your own life, or your church's, do you most need grace as strength rather than only as pardon?
Each Christian tradition says that salvation begins with God's grace. How might that shared conviction change the way you talk with Christians of another tradition?

title: Inductive Bible Study
summary: A way of studying a passage or book of the Bible that begins with careful observation of what the text actually says, moves to interpreting what it means in its context, correlates it with the rest of Scripture, and ends in applying it to life.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 17:10-12, what did the Jews of Beroea do with Paul's message, and how often?
Ezra 7:10 describes Ezra's commitment to God's law in three verbs. What are they, and why might the order matter?
James 1:22-25 compares a hearer who does not act to someone looking in a mirror. What point is James making about study and application?
Read Mark 4:35-41 slowly and list everything you observe before deciding what it means. What did you notice that you had missed before?
Which of the phases (observation, interpretation, correlation, application) do you tend to skip, and how could your group help you slow down?
steps: Pray for understanding, then choose a unit to study (a paragraph, a chapter or a whole short book) and read it through several times without notes or commentary.
Observe before you explain - write down who is involved, what happens or is argued, where and when, and note repeated words, contrasts, questions, turning points and the kind of writing it is.
Turn your observations into questions (what does this mean, why is it here, why is it said this way?) and answer them first from the passage and its surrounding book.
Only after your own study, check your conclusions against a good study Bible, Bible dictionary or commentary, and revise where the evidence points elsewhere.
Correlate the passage with the rest of Scripture, asking how other texts on the same subject, and the whole story centred on Christ, shed light on it.
Ask what the passage meant for its first readers and what it calls you to believe, pray or do now, and write down one concrete response.
Share what you found with others, ideally in a small group, so that your reading can be tested and enriched.

example.situation: A small group opens Mark 4:35-41, the stilling of the storm, during a hard season for one of its members.
example.before: This story promises that Jesus will make the storms in my life go away if I have enough faith.
example.after: The disciples end by asking who Jesus is, since even wind and sea obey him; the passage first shows his identity and calls me to trust him in the storm, whether or not it stops.
example.why: Observing the closing question (Mark 4:41) and its echo of God calming the sea in Psalm 107:29 moves the group from a quick application to the passage's own focus on who Jesus is.

title: Jeremiah's Temple Sermon
aliases: Jeremiah's sermon at the temple gate
the temple of the LORD sermon
summary: Jeremiah's message at the gate of the Jerusalem Temple (Jeremiah 7:1-15, with the story of its aftermath in Jeremiah 26), warning worshippers that chanting "the temple of the LORD" would not protect people who oppressed the vulnerable and broke the covenant, and that God could make the Temple like ruined Shiloh unless they changed their ways.
studyQuestions: Where does God tell Jeremiah to stand in Jeremiah 7:2, and who would be passing by as he spoke?
What were the people repeating in Jeremiah 7:4 and 7:10, and why did those words feel like a guarantee of safety?
Which wrongs does Jeremiah list in 7:5-9? How do they line up with the Ten Commandments and with care for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow?
Why does God send the listeners to look at Shiloh (7:12-14)? What had happened there?
In Jeremiah 26 the elders remember Micah's words about Zion (26:18-19). How does that memory save Jeremiah's life, and what does it suggest about how God's warnings work?
Jesus quotes Jeremiah 7:11 in the Temple (Mark 11:17). What does the original sermon add to your understanding of that scene?
What "safe words" or religious habits might a church or a believer lean on today instead of a changed life, and how could this passage gently correct that?

title: Jerusalem
summary: The hill city in the Judean highlands that David captured from the Jebusites and made his capital, where Solomon built the Temple; the centre of Israel's worship, the place of Jesus' death and resurrection and the starting point of the church's mission, and in the prophets and Revelation an image of God's people and his future dwelling with them.
studyQuestions: According to 2 Samuel 5:6-9, who lived in Jerusalem before David, and what did David call the stronghold once he took it?
Read Psalm 122. Why were pilgrims glad to go up to Jerusalem, and what does the psalmist ask readers to pray for?
In Isaiah 2:2-4, who comes to Jerusalem in the "latter days", and what do they go away with?
Luke 9:51 says Jesus "intently set his face" to go to Jerusalem, and Luke 19:41-44 shows him weeping over it. What do these two moments tell you about how Jesus regarded the city?
Revelation 21 describes a New Jerusalem with no temple in it. What does that suggest about where God means to live, and how might that hope shape the way you worship now?

title: Kingdom of God
summary: God's active reign as King, celebrated in the Old Testament, announced by Jesus as "at hand" in his own words and deeds, and awaited in its fullness when God's will is done on earth as in heaven; the central theme of Jesus's preaching in the first three Gospels.
studyQuestions: According to Mark 1:14-15, what does Jesus announce when he begins preaching in Galilee, and what two responses does he ask for?
In Luke 11:20, what does Jesus point to as a sign that God's Kingdom "has come to you"?
What do the parables of the seed growing by itself and the mustard seed (Mark 4:26-32) suggest about how God's Kingdom grows, and who makes it grow?
Psalm 145:13 calls God's Kingdom everlasting, yet Jesus teaches us to pray "Let your Kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10). How can both be true?
When you pray the Lord's Prayer, where in your own life, family or church do you most long to see God's will done "as in heaven, so on earth"?

title: Laying the Foundation of the Second Temple
aliases: rebuilding of the altar after the exile
joy and weeping at the Temple foundation
summary: Ezra 3:1-13, where the exiles who returned from Babylon rebuild the altar, keep the Feast of Tabernacles, and lay the foundation of a new Temple in Jerusalem, while the old who remembered Solomon's Temple weep and the young shout for joy so that the two sounds cannot be told apart.
studyQuestions: According to Ezra 3:2-6, what did the returned exiles build first, and what did they begin doing even though the Temple's foundation "was not yet laid"?
Ezra 3:3 says the people built the altar while "fear was on them". What does it suggest that they worshipped anyway?
What did the priests and Levites sing when the foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11), and where else in Scripture does that refrain appear?
Why did the older priests and Levites weep in Ezra 3:12? How does Haggai 2:3-9 speak to the same feeling?

Have you known a moment, in your own life or your church's, when joy and grief were mixed together so that you "could not discern" one from the other? What does this passage give you to bring to such a moment?

title: The Lord's Prayer
summary: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples, given in a longer form in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13) and a shorter one in Luke 11:2-4: an address to God as Father followed by petitions for his name, kingdom and will, and for daily bread, forgiveness and deliverance — prayed by Christians of every tradition ever since.
studyQuestions: Compare Matthew 6:9-13 with Luke 11:2-4. Which petitions do both share, and what setting does each Gospel give the prayer (Matthew 6:5-8; Luke 11:1)?
The first petitions are about God's name, kingdom and will; the later ones about our bread, our sins and our testing. What does that order teach about how to pray?
Every pronoun in the prayer is plural ("our", "us"). How does praying it change if I picture my church, or the believers I find hardest to love, praying it with me?
In Matthew 6:14-15 Jesus adds a comment on just one petition. Which one, and why might he single it out?
Jesus prays "your desire be done" in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:42). How does that scene deepen what it means to pray "your will be done"?

title: Moses
summary: The Levite raised in Pharaoh's household whom God called at the burning bush to lead Israel out of Egypt; he mediated the covenant and the law at Sinai, interceded for the people through forty years in the wilderness and died within sight of the promised land, remembered as the prophet with whom the LORD spoke face to face.
studyQuestions: According to Exodus 3:7-12, what has God seen and heard, what will he do, and how does he answer Moses' question "Who am I"?
What excuse does Moses give in Exodus 4:10, and how does God respond in verses 11-17?
In Exodus 32:11-14 and 32:30-32, what reasons does Moses give God for sparing the people? What does his prayer show about the kind of leader he was?
Why was Moses not allowed to lead Israel into the land (Numbers 20:7-12)? What exactly had God told him to do, and what did he do instead?
Hebrews 3:5-6 calls Moses a faithful servant in God's house and Christ a faithful Son over it. How does that comparison honour Moses rather than dismiss him?
Moses argued with God, failed, interceded and kept going for forty years. Where in your own calling do you most identify with his reluctance — or with his perseverance?

title: Paul
summary: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who persecuted the first Christians, met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles; he planted churches across the eastern Mediterranean, and the letters bearing his name make up nearly half the books of the New Testament.
studyQuestions: In Acts 9:1-6, what is Saul doing when Jesus meets him, and what question does Jesus ask him?
Compare Acts 9:20-30 with Galatians 1:15-24. What does each account emphasise about what Paul did after his conversion?
In Philippians 3:4-8, which credentials does Paul list, and how does he now value them?
Paul calls himself "the least of the apostles" yet says God's grace was not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:9-10). How might his story shape the way we see people who have done harm, or our own past?

title: Paul at the Areopagus
summary: Paul's visit to Athens and his speech before the Areopagus in Acts 17:16-34, where he takes an altar "to the unknown god" as his starting point and proclaims the Creator who does not live in temples, who made all nations, and who now calls everyone to repent before the day he will judge the world through the man he raised from the dead.
studyQuestions: What did Paul see in Athens that "stirred" his spirit (Acts 17:16), and where did he go to talk with people (17:17)?
Why did some listeners think Paul was proclaiming "strange gods" (17:18)? What two things had he been preaching?
Paul quotes a Greek poet in Acts 17:28. What point does he draw from the line in the next verse (17:29)?
The speech begins with creation and ends with repentance, judgment and the resurrection (17:30-31). Why do you think Paul builds toward Jesus in that order for this audience?
Luke records three responses in 17:32-34. Which response do you see most often when you talk about faith with friends or colleagues, and what might Paul's example teach you about those conversations?

title: Pharisees
summary: A Jewish movement of the Second Temple period known for careful interpretation and practice of the Torah, the "tradition of the elders" and belief in the resurrection; Jesus's frequent conversation partners and critics in the Gospels, Paul's own party, and forerunners of the later rabbis.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 23:6-8, which beliefs did the Pharisees hold that the Sadducees rejected?
In Matthew 23:2-3, what does Jesus tell the crowds to do with the Pharisees' teaching, and what does he warn them not to copy?
Nicodemus (John 3:1-2) and Gamaliel (Acts 5:34-39) were both Pharisees. How do their stories complicate the picture of the Pharisees as simply Jesus's enemies?
Jesus's sharpest warnings were aimed at devout, Bible-loving people. Where might Matthew 23:23-28 speak to our own church life today?

title: Reading in Context
aliases: a text without a context is a pretext
summary: The basic interpretive habit of reading any verse within its surrounding passage, its book, the whole of Scripture and its original historical and cultural setting, so that it means what its author meant before we ask what it means for us.
studyQuestions: According to Jeremiah 29:1-10, who first received the letter containing verse 11, where were they, and how long did God say they would wait?
Read Philippians 4:10-14. What "all things" is Paul talking about in verse 13, and how does that change the way the verse is often used?
Revelation 3:20 is often used in evangelism. To whom is it first addressed (Revelation 3:14-22), and what does that add to its meaning?
Which verse do you hold dear but have never read in its surrounding chapter, and what do you notice when you read the whole chapter this week?
steps: Read the whole paragraph, and then the whole chapter, around the verse before deciding what it means.
Ask who is speaking, to whom, and in what situation; note what the book itself tells you about its author and first readers.
Trace the flow of thought by asking what comes just before, what comes just after, and how the verse fits the argument or story.
Identify the kind of writing (letter, poem, prophecy, narrative) and read it the way that kind of writing is meant to be read.
Use a study Bible or Bible dictionary to fill in historical and cultural background, without letting the background drown out the text.
Compare the passage with other Scripture on the same subject, especially clearer passages, and see how it fits the whole story that centres on Christ.
Only then ask what the passage means for you or your church, applying it in a way its first readers would recognise as faithful to it.

example.situation: A friend facing a job interview posts Jeremiah 29:11 as a guarantee that everything will go well.
example.before: God has promised me success and no setbacks, so this interview is bound to work out.
example.after: God told exiles in Babylon to settle in and seek the city's peace, promising a future after seventy years; I can trust his good purposes and be faithful where I am, even if this interview fails.
example.why: Reading the whole letter (Jeremiah 29:1-14) shows a promise of long-range hope to a community in exile, which still comforts believers today but not as a pledge of quick personal success.

title: Second Temple Judaism
aliases: Judaism of the Second Temple period
the Jews' religion in Jesus's day
summary: The faith and life of the Jewish people from the rebuilding of the Jerusalem Temple (515 BC) to its destruction by Rome (AD 70), centred on the one God, the Torah and the Temple yet varied in its parties and hopes; the world of Ezra, the Maccabees, Jesus, the apostles and Paul.
studyQuestions: According to Nehemiah 8:1-8, what did Ezra and the Levites do with the Law of Moses, and how did the people respond?
In Luke 4:16-21, what does Jesus do "as was his custom" on the Sabbath, and what does that tell us about his own Jewish practice?
Acts 23:6-8 shows Pharisees and Sadducees disagreeing about the resurrection. What does that suggest about how varied Jewish belief was in Paul's day?
Which familiar Gospel scenes (a synagogue reading, a Temple feast, a debate with Pharisees) do you now picture differently, and why might knowing Jesus's Jewish world deepen your reading of him?

title: Septuagint
summary: The ancient Greek translation of Israel's Scriptures, begun with the Pentateuch in Egypt in the third century BC; it was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the first Christians, is quoted throughout the New Testament, and remains the Old Testament of the Orthodox Church.
studyQuestions: Compare Psalm 40:6 in an English Bible with Hebrews 10:5. What does each say God prepared, and why might they differ?
In Acts 15:17, how does James's quotation of Amos 9:12 support welcoming Gentiles, and how does the Hebrew wording of Amos read?
Why do you think the apostles were content to quote Scripture in a translation their hearers could understand?
How might knowing about the Septuagint help you talk graciously with a Christian whose Old Testament has more books than yours?

title: Sermon on the Mount
summary: Jesus's longest continuous teaching in the Gospels (Matthew 5–7), given on a mountain in Galilee: the Beatitudes, salt and light, the fulfilment of the Law, almsgiving, prayer and fasting, the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule and the closing call to hear and do his words.
studyQuestions: Who is listening when Jesus begins to teach in Matthew 5:1-2, and who is listening when he finishes in Matthew 7:28-29? Why might both groups matter?
In Matthew 5:17-20, what does Jesus say he came to do with the Law and the Prophets?
Read the three examples of "secret" devotion in Matthew 6:1-18 (giving, prayer, fasting). What do they have in common, and which one most challenges your own habits?
The sermon ends with two builders (Matthew 7:24-27). What is the difference between them, and what would "doing" one of these teachings look like for you or your group this week?

title: The Exodus
summary: God's deliverance of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt under Moses — through the plagues, the first Passover and the crossing of the sea — which became Israel's defining story of salvation and which the New Testament uses to explain the death and resurrection of Jesus.
studyQuestions: In Exodus 3:7-8, what four things does God say he has seen, heard, known and come down to do for his people?
According to Exodus 12:26-27, what are parents to tell their children when they ask about the Passover, and why might Israel have built a question into the ritual?
How does Exodus 20:2 connect the commandments to the rescue from Egypt? What difference does it make that God saves first and then gives the law?

Paul calls Christ "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7) and says the wilderness events "happened to them by way of example" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Where do you see your own story in Israel's — both the rescue and the grumbling afterwards?

title: The Story of the Bible
summary: The single, unfolding story that Christians read across the Bible's many books: God creates a good world, humanity turns away, God calls Abraham and Israel, comes in Jesus the Messiah, sends the church to all nations, and promises a renewed creation.
studyQuestions: In Genesis 12:1-3, what does God promise Abram, and who will finally be blessed through him?
According to Luke 24:27 and Luke 24:44, which parts of the Scriptures did the risen Jesus say were about him?
Compare Genesis 3:23-24 with Revelation 22:1-3. What was lost at the beginning of the story, and what is restored at the end?
Why might it matter whether the Old Testament closes with Cyrus's call to "go up" (2 Chronicles 36:23) or with the promise of Elijah (Malachi 4:5)?
If the church lives in the "act" between Pentecost and the new creation, what would faithful "improvising" look like in your own congregation this year?
